nameStory: The name 'cinquefoil' comes from the French 'cinq feuilles,' meaning 'five leaves,' referring to the plant's signature five leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand. The 'common' part distinguishes it from its many cousins in the cinquefoil family, as this species is indeed one of the most widespread and frequently encountered in New England.
description: Common cinquefoil is a low-growing perennial wildflower that spreads along the ground by runners, much like a strawberry plant. It produces cheerful bright yellow flowers with five rounded petals from spring into early summer. The plant stays quite small, rarely growing more than a few inches tall, but can spread several feet across as it sends out new runners that root wherever they touch the ground.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Five leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, rising from runners on separate stalks from the flowers. Each leaflet feels smooth and has a soft, slightly fuzzy texture with visible veining.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with exactly five rounded petals that feel delicate and papery to the touch. Flowers are small, about the size of a dime, and sit on individual stalks.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Creeps along the ground with prostrate stems that root at joints, creating new plants as it spreads. The runners feel firm and slightly reddish, similar to strawberry runners.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, dry seed clusters that replace the flowers by midsummer. Unlike strawberries, these fruits are hard and not fleshy.

habitat: Common cinquefoil thrives in poor, thin soils where other plants struggle, making it a reliable indicator of impoverished ground. Look for it in old fields, woodland edges, disturbed areas, and along trails where the soil is sandy, rocky, or has been compacted. It's particularly common in areas that have been cleared or disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Bright yellow flowers begin appearing in March and continue through May, making this one of the earlier wildflowers to bloom. New leaves emerge fresh and green from overwintered runners.
seasonality.summer: Flowering continues into June, with seed production following. The plant continues spreading via runners throughout the growing season, creating new patches.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn reddish or bronze before dying back. Seeds are mature and dispersing, while runners remain active until frost.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, but the root system and some runners persist under the soil, ready to send up new growth in spring.

funFact: Common cinquefoil is essentially nature's soil tester - when you see large patches of it, you're looking at ground that's too poor for most other plants to thrive, making it a living indicator that the soil lacks nutrients or has been heavily disturbed.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with wild strawberry, which also has five leaflets and spreads by runners. The key difference: strawberries have white flowers and produce red, fleshy berries, while cinquefoil has yellow flowers and dry seed clusters. Remember: yellow flowers = cinquefoil, white flowers = strawberry.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'five-fingers' and having five leaflets, don't confuse this with the tropical houseplant also called five-finger. Common cinquefoil is a true New England native and completely hardy outdoors, while the houseplant five-finger is tropical and unrelated.
compareHints: Common cinquefoil differs from dwarf cinquefoil by its longer, more obvious runners and slightly larger flowers. Unlike sulphur cinquefoil, which grows upright, common cinquefoil hugs the ground. It's distinguished from mock strawberry by having yellow rather than white flowers and by producing dry seeds instead of red berry-like fruits.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sulphur cinquefoil stands out from other New England cinquefoils primarily by its bright yellow flowers and consistently five-fingered leaves.

Among New England's cinquefoils, silvery cinquefoil is the only one with dramatically silver-white fuzzy leaf undersides - dwarf and common cinquefoil have plain green undersides, while rough cinquefoil has much larger, coarsely-toothed leaves.
Among New England's cinquefoils, dwarf cinquefoil is distinguished by its truly prostrate, mat-forming habit with rooting runners.
Unlike other cinquefoils in its genus which typically have five-part leaves (the name cinquefoil means 'five leaves'), mock strawberry has three-part leaves like true strawberries.
Unlike most other New England cinquefoils which have five leaflets, rough cinquefoil stands out with just three leaflets per leaf.
Lesser mock-strawberry differs from other cinquefoils by having three-part leaves instead of the typical five-part leaves (cinque means five in French).
Unlike its lowland cinquefoil relatives that spread by runners or grow as larger plants, dwarf mountain cinquefoil forms tiny, tight cushions and never leaves the alpine zone.

Among New England's cinquefoils, creeping cinquefoil is unique for its long trailing runners and five-leaflet leaves – most other cinquefoils like common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have three leaflets and don't spread by runners.

Intermediate cinquefoil differs from common New England cinquefoils like dwarf cinquefoil by its specific leaflet count and arrangement, and from sulphur cinquefoil by its smaller stature and different leaf texture.
Unlike its inland cinquefoil relatives, coast cinquefoil has adapted specifically to maritime conditions with its more compact, mat-forming growth and thicker, more succulent-like leaves.
